title: I let an agent run 893 bots on a paper desk. This morning I counted what my stop-losses actually did, and 92% of them filled past the number I set.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Quick disclosure so nobody has to guess: I built the platform this runs on, these are my own bots, and it is all paper money. Not linking anything.

I have been posting my fleet's ugly numbers here for a couple of weeks — 24,908 closed trades, down $1,056,151. Yesterday someone pushed me on exit logic, so this morning I pulled the exits apart instead of the entries. The result is the most useful thing I have measured yet.

Stop-losses are 1.04% of my trades and 39.4% of my losses.

259 stop-loss exits out of 24,908. They account for $415,748 of the $1,056,151. That alone was worth knowing.

But the part I did not expect was WHERE they filled. For 149 of them I could read the bot's own configured stop and compare it to the actual exit:

- Median stop configured: −35%
- Median exit actually taken: −40.5%
- Filled past the stop: 137 of 149, so 92%
- Worst single case: a −30% stop that got out at −78.5%
- Filled BETTER than the stop: zero

Not one of 149. The distribution has a hard wall at your stop and a long tail to the wrong side of it.

Stocks, same query, same fleet: 70 stop exits, 41% overshot, median 0.3 points past. So this is not a general "stops don't work" claim. It is specifically an options problem.

Why, and this is the boring part that matters. A stop in my engine is an overlay checked once per the strategy's own bar. That is documented, it is the default, and there is an opt-in \`check: "minute"\` setting that sweeps every minute instead. Of the 950 bots deployed on my desk, the number using it is zero. Including all the ones the agent built itself, because the agent had no reason to change a default that looked fine.

So a bot on a 4-hour bar that crosses its stop at 10:05 acts on it at 13:30. On a stock that is usually a rounding error. On an option, premium can move 30 points in that gap.

Some of the overshoot is my own modeled spread — the engine sells at the real bid, or last minus 2.5% when there is no quote. But for 69 of the 149, the overshoot was larger than the entire 5% round-trip spread, so the spread does not explain it.

What I actually take from this: if your backtest models a −30% stop as exiting at exactly −30%, it is optimistic, and on options it is optimistic by about 5 points at the median. Mine was. That is a real gap between the thing I promised the bot and the thing the bot got.

Happy to go into the query or the distribution. The card in the image is every one of the 149 as a dot.
